note: 50 questions, all one level. Built for surprise while staying guessable. Every citation points at a source retrieved during research.

questions.prompt: How many people still have no electricity at all?
questions.whyCorrect: 666.4 million people live without electricity — no light after sunset, no fridge, no way to charge anything.
whyWrong: Ten times too low.
A hundred times too low.
questions.action: Count everything in your home that needs electricity.

questions.prompt: How many people cook using polluting fuels like wood, charcoal or dung?
questions.whyCorrect: 2.1 billion people — over a quarter of the world. The smoke causes serious lung disease, mostly among women and children.
whyWrong: A hundred times too low.
Ten times too low.
questions.action: Find out what fuel cooked your last meal.

questions.prompt: What share of the world's electricity deficit is in sub-Saharan Africa?
questions.whyCorrect: 85% — some 565 million of the 666 million unconnected people live there. Electricity access is overwhelmingly one region's problem.
whyWrong: Far too low — the concentration is extreme.
Vastly too low.
questions.action: Find sub-Saharan Africa on a map.

questions.prompt: Where do most people without electricity live?
questions.whyCorrect: 84% live in rural communities. Running power lines to scattered villages costs far more per household than wiring a city.
whyWrong: Cities are far easier and cheaper to connect.
Not a defining pattern for energy access.
questions.action: Ask why it's expensive to connect a remote village.

questions.prompt: What share of the world now has electricity?
questions.whyCorrect: 92%, up from 84% in 2010. Huge progress — and still 666 million people short.
whyWrong: Too pessimistic — access has improved substantially.
Too optimistic — hundreds of millions remain unconnected.
questions.action: Compare 84% in 2010 with 92% today.

questions.prompt: In sub-Saharan Africa, what share of people can cook with clean fuels?
questions.whyCorrect: Only 21% — against a global average of 74%. Nearly four in five people there still cook over smoke.
whyWrong: Far too optimistic for the region.
That's closer to the global average.
questions.action: Compare 21% regionally with 74% globally.

questions.prompt: What share of the world's total energy comes from renewables?
questions.whyCorrect: 17.9% of all final energy — much lower than people expect, because heating and transport still run mostly on fossil fuels.
whyWrong: Far too optimistic across all energy uses.
Too pessimistic — renewables are approaching a fifth.
questions.action: Ask why the renewable share of ALL energy is lower than for electricity.

questions.prompt: What share of the world's ELECTRICITY comes from renewables?
questions.whyCorrect: 30% — much higher than the 17.9% share of total energy, because electricity is the easiest sector to decarbonise.
whyWrong: Too pessimistic — renewables generate nearly a third of electricity.
Too optimistic globally.
questions.action: Find out where your electricity comes from.

questions.prompt: What share of TRANSPORT energy is renewable?
questions.whyCorrect: Just 4%. Cars, trucks, ships and planes remain almost entirely fossil-fuelled — the hardest sector to change.
whyWrong: Ten times too optimistic.
Far too optimistic for transport.
questions.action: Count how many electric vehicles you saw today.

questions.prompt: How many people will still lack electricity in 2030 on current trends?
questions.whyCorrect: 645 million — barely better than today's 666 million. Population growth is nearly cancelling out new connections.
whyWrong: That's the target, not the projection.
The projection is more than ten times higher.
questions.action: Ask why connecting people gets harder as you go.

questions.prompt: How many people will still cook with polluting fuels in 2030?
questions.whyCorrect: 1.8 billion — only slightly better than today's 2.1 billion. Clean cooking is one of the most badly off-track targets.
whyWrong: Ten times too low.
That's the target, not the projection.
questions.action: Ask what a family needs to switch cooking fuel.

questions.prompt: How much clean energy finance did developing countries receive in 2023?
questions.whyCorrect: $21.6 billion — a large sum, but small against the scale of connecting 666 million people and switching 2.1 billion to clean cooking.
whyWrong: Ten times too high.
Ten times too low.
questions.action: Compare that with what your country spends on roads.

questions.prompt: Which technology got the biggest share of clean energy finance?
questions.whyCorrect: Solar took $9.4 billion of the $21.6 billion — 44% of all clean energy flows to developing countries.
whyWrong: Not a significant share of these flows.
Coal isn't clean energy finance.
questions.action: Ask why solar suits places without existing power grids.

questions.prompt: Energy efficiency improved 2.1% in 2022. What rate is needed?
questions.whyCorrect: 4% annually through 2030 — nearly double the current pace. Efficiency is the cheapest form of clean energy, and it's lagging.
whyWrong: Below the current rate.
That's roughly the current rate, not the target.
questions.action: Name three ways to use less energy for the same result.

questions.prompt: Clean cooking access rose from 64% in 2015 to what today?
questions.whyCorrect: 74% — ten percentage points in eight years. Real progress, still leaving 2.1 billion people cooking over smoke.
whyWrong: Too optimistic — over a quarter of the world lacks it.
The improvement was larger than this.
questions.action: Ask what health problems wood smoke causes indoors.

questions.prompt: How many people in sub-Saharan Africa have no electricity?
questions.whyCorrect: 565 million — 85% of the global total, in one region.
whyWrong: Ten times too low.
A hundred times too low.
questions.action: Compare 565 million with your country's population.

questions.prompt: Excluding traditional wood burning, modern renewables grew from 10% to what?
questions.whyCorrect: 13% — a three-point gain. Distinguishing modern renewables from traditional biomass matters, because burning wood isn't clean energy.
whyWrong: That's the renewable share of electricity, not total energy.
Far too optimistic.
questions.action: Ask why burning wood counts as renewable but isn't clean.

questions.prompt: Why is clean cooking a health issue, not just an energy one?
options: Smoke from cooking fires causes serious lung disease
questions.whyCorrect: Indoor smoke from wood, charcoal and dung causes respiratory illness and premature death, hitting women and young children hardest since they're near the fire.
whyWrong: Household air pollution is a major cause of death.
The issue is health, not flavour.
questions.action: Ask who in a household spends most time near the stove.

questions.prompt: Electricity access rose 8 points since 2010. Is that enough for universal access by 2030?
options: No — 645 million will still lack it
questions.whyCorrect: Projections show 645 million still unconnected in 2030, barely down from 666 million today. Progress is being eaten by population growth.
whyWrong: The projection misses the target by hundreds of millions.
The gap barely closes.
questions.action: Ask what makes the last 8% hardest to reach.

questions.prompt: Which sector is furthest from renewable energy?
questions.whyCorrect: Transport at 4%, against 30% for electricity. Batteries and fuels for planes, ships and trucks are far harder problems than power stations.
whyWrong: There's a 26-point gap.
Electricity is the most advanced sector.
questions.action: Ask what would have to change for planes to run clean.

questions.prompt: Roughly what share of the world cooks with polluting fuels?
questions.whyCorrect: With 74% having clean cooking access, about 26% — over a quarter of humanity — still cook over polluting fuels.
whyWrong: Vastly too optimistic.
Too high — most people do have clean cooking.
questions.action: Ask what 'clean cooking' actually requires.

questions.prompt: Solar received $9.4 billion of clean energy finance. Why does solar suit developing countries?
options: It only works in cold places
It works without an existing grid
questions.whyCorrect: Solar panels can power a home or village without waiting for national grid lines — which matters when 84% of unconnected people live rurally.
whyWrong: That's the advantage of solar — it doesn't need one.
Solar performs best in sunny regions.
questions.action: Ask what a single solar panel can run.

questions.prompt: Global electricity access in 2010 was:
questions.whyCorrect: 84%, rising to 92% by 2023 — eight percentage points in thirteen years.
whyWrong: Too optimistic for 2010.
Too pessimistic — access was already high.
questions.action: Work out the annual rate of improvement.

questions.prompt: Energy intensity improved 2.1% in 2022. What does 'energy intensity' mean?
options: Energy used per unit of economic output
questions.whyCorrect: It measures how much energy an economy needs to produce a given amount of value — falling intensity means more output from less energy.
whyWrong: That's total consumption, not intensity.
Not related to the measure.
questions.action: Ask how a factory could make the same goods with less power.

questions.prompt: Which is closest to the truth about renewable energy?
options: Nearly a third of electricity, but under a fifth of all energy
questions.whyCorrect: 30% of electricity but only 17.9% of total energy — because heating, industry and transport still burn fossil fuels directly.
whyWrong: Far too optimistic across all energy uses.
Far too pessimistic — renewables are substantial.
questions.action: List three energy uses in your home that aren't electricity.

questions.prompt: If 92% have electricity, how many don't?
questions.whyCorrect: 666.4 million people. Eight percent of eight billion is a very large number of human beings.
whyWrong: Vastly too low.
Ten times too low.
questions.action: Always convert a percentage into people.

questions.prompt: Clean cooking is projected to reach what share by 2030?
questions.whyCorrect: Only 78%, up from 74% today — a four-point gain in six years, leaving 1.8 billion people behind.
whyWrong: Coverage is already above this.
That's the target, not the projection.
questions.action: Ask why clean cooking progress is so slow.

questions.prompt: What makes rural electrification expensive?
options: Long power lines serving few households
questions.whyCorrect: Grid extension costs the same per kilometre whether it serves 500 households or 5. With 84% of unconnected people rural, that economics is the core barrier.
whyWrong: Many rural regions have excellent solar potential.
Rural households typically use far less power.
questions.action: Ask whether a mini-grid could beat a long power line.

questions.prompt: How much of clean energy finance did solar NOT receive?
questions.whyCorrect: Solar took 44%, so about 56% — roughly $12.2 billion — went to wind, hydro, geothermal and other technologies.
whyWrong: Solar took 44%, leaving far more than 5%.
Solar's share was substantial at 44%.
questions.action: Name three renewable technologies other than solar.

questions.prompt: Which Goal 7 measure is furthest off track?
options: Clean cooking — 1.8 billion still without by 2030
questions.whyCorrect: Clean cooking. Electricity will reach 92%+ and renewables generate 30% of power, but 1.8 billion people are projected to still cook over smoke in 2030.
whyWrong: Access is at 92% and rising.
Renewables reached 30% of electricity.
questions.action: Ask why cooking is harder to change than lighting.

questions.prompt: Energy efficiency needs to improve 4% a year. Current rate is:
questions.whyCorrect: 2.1% against a needed 4% — roughly half the required pace.
whyWrong: The current rate is below target, not above.
There's a substantial shortfall.
questions.action: Ask what would double the world's efficiency gains.

questions.prompt: Traditional biomass is counted as renewable. Why is that misleading?
options: Burning wood indoors still causes disease and deforestation
questions.whyCorrect: Wood regrows, so it counts as renewable — but burning it indoors is exactly the polluting cooking that affects 2.1 billion people. Modern renewables are tracked separately at 13% for this reason.
whyWrong: Biomass does regrow, which is why it's classed as renewable.
Wood smoke is the main source of household air pollution.
questions.action: Ask what makes an energy source clean as well as renewable.

questions.prompt: How many people gained electricity access between 2010 and 2023?
questions.whyCorrect: Access rose from 84% to 92% while the population grew — meaning well over a billion people gained electricity in that period.
whyWrong: Access improved by 8 percentage points.
Vastly too low.
questions.action: Ask what changes in a household the year it gets power.

questions.prompt: Which region has the lowest clean cooking access?
questions.whyCorrect: Sub-Saharan Africa at 21% — the same region holding 85% of the world's electricity deficit.
whyWrong: East Asia has made major progress on clean cooking.
Europe has near-universal clean cooking.
questions.action: Ask why one region lags on both energy measures.

questions.prompt: Renewables are 30% of electricity. What's the other 70%?
questions.whyCorrect: Coal, gas, oil and nuclear make up the rest. Renewables have grown fast but still generate under a third of the world's power.
whyWrong: Electricity must be generated by something.
Electricity is mostly generated domestically.
questions.action: Look up your country's electricity mix.

questions.prompt: The world will likely miss Goal 7. What's the clearest evidence?
options: 645 million without power and 1.8 billion without clean cooking in 2030
questions.whyCorrect: Both projections leave enormous numbers behind at the deadline — despite genuine progress in access and renewables.
whyWrong: Electricity access rose from 84% to 92%.
Renewables reached 30% of electricity and are growing.
questions.action: Ask what would have to change to hit the target.

questions.prompt: What share of people without electricity live in cities?
questions.whyCorrect: Since 84% live rurally, about 16% of the unconnected are urban — a minority, but still over 100 million people.
whyWrong: That's the rural figure.
The split is heavily rural.
questions.action: Ask why some city dwellers still lack power.

questions.prompt: Modern renewables rose from 10% to 13%. Over roughly how long?
questions.whyCorrect: A three-point gain over several years — steady but far slower than the headlines about a renewable revolution suggest.
whyWrong: Modern renewables barely existed a century ago.
Energy systems change over years and decades.
questions.action: Ask why energy systems change slowly.

questions.prompt: $21.6 billion of clean energy finance sounds large. Compared to the need it is:
options: Small — hundreds of millions still need connecting
questions.whyCorrect: It has to serve 666 million people needing electricity and 2.1 billion needing clean cooking — a few dollars per person per year.
whyWrong: Projections show both targets being badly missed.
The financing gap is substantial.
questions.action: Divide $21.6bn by 2.1 billion people.

questions.prompt: Electricity access is 92% but clean cooking only 74%. Why the gap?
options: Cooking needs fuel supply chains, not just wires
questions.whyCorrect: A power line delivers electricity once built. Clean cooking needs affordable stoves plus a reliable, ongoing supply of gas or electricity a family can pay for every week.
whyWrong: Cooking is one of the largest household energy uses.
The barriers are cost and supply, not desire.
questions.action: Ask what your household pays to cook each month.

questions.prompt: Which is true about renewables in transport?
questions.whyCorrect: 4%. Despite electric cars getting attention, transport as a whole — including trucks, ships and planes — remains almost entirely fossil-fuelled.
whyWrong: Vastly too optimistic.
The overwhelming majority of transport burns fossil fuels.
questions.action: Count the vehicles you saw today and guess how many were electric.

questions.prompt: If sub-Saharan Africa is 85% of the electricity deficit, what does that mean for solutions?
options: Progress there decides the global result
questions.whyCorrect: With 565 of 666 million unconnected people there, global energy access is essentially a sub-Saharan Africa question.
whyWrong: It holds the overwhelming majority of the problem.
No other region comes close.
questions.action: Ask what would connect 565 million people fastest.

questions.prompt: Global electricity access target for 2030 is universal. Projection says:
questions.whyCorrect: 645 million people still unconnected — the target will be missed by a wide margin without a major acceleration.
whyWrong: The projection falls well short.
Access is projected to keep improving, just too slowly.
questions.action: Compare 666 million today with 645 million projected.

questions.prompt: Why is energy efficiency called the cheapest clean energy?
options: Energy you don't use costs nothing and emits nothing
questions.whyCorrect: The cleanest kilowatt is the one never generated. That's why the 4% annual efficiency target matters as much as building renewables.
whyWrong: Efficiency is consistently the lowest-cost option per unit of carbon saved.
Efficiency measures do cost money upfront.
questions.action: Find one thing at home wasting energy right now.

questions.prompt: Clean cooking access in sub-Saharan Africa versus the world:
questions.whyCorrect: 21% regionally against 74% globally — a 53-point gap, the widest of any Goal 7 measure.
whyWrong: It's the other way round.
The gap is enormous, not equal.
questions.action: Ask what would change cooking fuel for 500 million people.

questions.prompt: Renewable energy is 17.9% of total energy. Ten years ago it was:
questions.whyCorrect: Modern renewables rose from 10% to 13% over recent years, so the total share has been climbing — steadily but not dramatically.
whyWrong: There has been measurable growth.
Renewables have grown, not shrunk.
questions.action: Ask what would make renewables grow faster.

questions.prompt: Who suffers most from cooking smoke?
questions.whyCorrect: Women do most cooking in most households, often with young children nearby — so household air pollution falls hardest on them.
whyWrong: Men are affected too, but spend less time at the stove.
Household air pollution causes millions of premature deaths.
questions.action: Ask who cooks in your home and for how long.

questions.prompt: Global electricity access is 92%. What does the remaining 8% represent?
questions.whyCorrect: 85% of the deficit is sub-Saharan Africa and 84% of unconnected people are rural — the two facts overlap almost completely.
whyWrong: Europe has near-universal access.
Wealthy areas are connected.
questions.action: Ask what 'last mile' means in infrastructure.

questions.prompt: Which had the bigger improvement since 2015: electricity or clean cooking?
questions.whyCorrect: Clean cooking rose 10 points from 64% to 74%; electricity rose 8 points from 84% to 92% (measured from 2010). Cooking improved faster but from much further behind.
whyWrong: Clean cooking gained more percentage points.
Both improved substantially.
questions.action: Ask whether starting further behind makes gains easier or harder.

questions.prompt: What's the most surprising thing about Goal 7?
options: Renewables are 30% of electricity but only 4% of transport
questions.whyCorrect: The clean energy transition is real in power stations and barely started in transport — a 26-point gap between the two sectors.
whyWrong: Both access targets are projected to be badly missed.
Electricity access rose to 92% and renewables to 30% of power.
questions.action: Ask which sector you'd focus on next, and why.
